power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Introduction: Recent research has increasingly adopted complex dynamical systems theory to understand psychopathology.
A key proposition is that psychopathological symptoms may operate at different time scales, with different dynamic speeds shaping the evolution of the symptom system.
This study examined the extent to which variability in symptom dynamic speed reflects symptom differences, person differences, and person-by-symptom interactions.
Methods: We analyzed five intensive longitudinal experience sampling datasets comprising 265 participants and 33,059 retained observations.
Dynamic speed was quantified for each person-symptom time series using lag-1 autocorrelation (AC) and mean period (MP) derived from Lomb-Scargle spectral analysis.
Multilevel variance decomposition was used to partition variability into person, symptom, and person-by-symptom components.
Results: Across the two dynamic speed indices, symptom variance was generally nonsignificant.

Person variance and person-by-symptom interaction variance were significant in several datasets and generally exceeded symptom variance, although pairwise differences between variance components were not consistently significant.
The findings provide limited evidence for consistent symptom differences in dynamic speed; person differences and person-by-symptom interactions may play a more prominent role.
These results highlight the importance of idiographic approaches to understanding symptom dynamics and underscore the need for further research into the clinical implications of dynamic speed.

In recent years, clinical psychology has increasingly adopted a complex dynamical systems perspective to study psychopathology, conceptualizing psychopathological symptom systems as composed of multiple dynamic processes-i.e., different psychopathological symptoms-that continuously evolve over time (Borsboom, 2017; Olthof et al., 2023; Robinaugh et al., 2026; Scheffer et al., 2024a Scheffer et al., , 2024b;; Zhang et al., 2026).

text.text: This distinction between fast and slow variables helps characterize the dynamic organization of complex dynamical systems: faster processes may respond more rapidly to external perturbations or changes in the internal state of the system, whereas slower processes may shape or constrain changes in fast variables and their responses to external perturbations over longer time scales, thereby influencing system stability and state transitions (Carpenter & Turner, 2000; Hasselman, 2023; Walker et al., 2012).

text.text: For example, in a lake ecosystem, phosphorus concentration can be considered a slow variable, whereas algae can be considered a fast variable (Carpenter & Turner, 2000; Rinaldi & Scheffer, 2000).

text.text: When phosphorus concentration has not yet crossed a critical threshold, algae may fluctuate rapidly, but their fluctuations remain constrained within a certain range, and the system remains in a clearwater state.

As phosphorus concentration gradually increases and crosses the critical threshold, however, algae may change abruptly, and the system may suddenly shift from a clear-water state to a turbid-water state.

text.text: Their development may take longer, and interventions targeting them may require greater effort.
In contrast, if some symptoms function as fast variables, they may reflect state-like fluctuations and may respond more rapidly to external stimuli or interventions.

Thus, understanding the relative dynamic speed of symptoms may help distinguish different elements within a psychopathological symptom system and provide insights into psychopathological mechanisms, prevention, and intervention.

Taking depression as an example, it comprises symptoms spanning different domains, including affective symptoms (e.g., depressed mood), self-evaluative symptoms (e.g., guilt and feelings of worthlessness), and physiological symptoms (e.g., appetite and sleep) (American Psychiatric Association, 2022).

text.text: At the same time, whether the dynamic speed of psychopathological symptoms has a general and consistent pattern across individuals remains unclear.

In recent years, clinical psychology has increasingly emphasized individual heterogeneity in psychological processes and the importance of idiographic research (Molenaar, 2004; Piccirillo & Rodebaugh, 2019; Wright & Woods, 2020).

text.text: Intensive longitudinal studies have also shown substantial individual differences in the dynamics of psychological symptoms, suggesting that the same symptom may exhibit different dynamic characteristics across individuals (Ebrahimi et al., 2021; Fisher et al., 2017; Nemesure et al., 2024; Reeves & Fisher, 2020).

text.text: However, to our knowledge, no study has systematically examined whether differences in the dynamic speed of psychopathological symptoms arise primarily from individual differences, symptom differences, or person-by-symptom interactions.
The present study therefore addresses this question.
As an exploratory study, we did not formulate specific hypotheses.

text.text: To capture the dynamic speed of psychopathological symptoms, the present study used data from a longitudinal experience sampling design, in which individuals were asked to report their psychopathological symptoms repeatedly at a predetermined frequency over a specified period.

We used four publicly available datasets from the OpenESM platform (https://openesmdata.org/; Siepe et al., 2026), namely Bailon et al. (2020 ), Fisher et al. (2017), Reeves & Fisher (2020), and Wang et al. (2016).

text.text: In the following, these datasets are identified by their first authors.
In addition, we collected a dataset ourselves, which we refer to as Dataset E. All procedures were reviewed and approved by the ethics committee of the first author's institution.
We recruited middle school students from southern China.
In early March 2026, before a mental health class began, we announced our study.
The study was described as recording daily mental health states, and recruitment was announced; interested students could participate.
Participants were included based on active participation and informed consent from both themselves and their guardians.
They completed a paper-and-pencil questionnaire for approximately 15 minutes each evening before going to bed for 90 consecutive days, continuing until mid-June 2026.
Participants could withdraw at any time and received a small snack as a reward after each completed assessment.
Seventy-five participants took part in the study, of whom 70 reported their gender and age (37 girls, 33 boys; mean age = 12.943 years, SD = 0.778, range = 12-15 years).

The Reeves dataset focused on PTSD symptoms; the Fisher dataset and Dataset E focused on depressive and anxiety symptoms and related symptoms; and the Bailon dataset focused on current affect (unidimensional, negative to positive) and subjective physical activity, two relatively broad indicators.

Although these two do not directly belong to a specific disorder, they are often included as indicators in psychopathology research (e.g., long-term negative affect and long-term psychomotor retardation in depressed patients; American Psychiatric Association, 2022).

Because the present study focuses on the dynamic speed of psychopathological symptoms, these two indicators may reflect the distinction between affect and subjective bodily sensations as two broad categories of psychopathological symptoms.

Therefore, in this study, we also roughly treated them as psychopathological symptoms, which is to some extent consistent with current scholarly discussions of psychopathological symptoms as multi-level and broad categories (Kotov et al., 2017).

In this study, the speed of symptom fluctuations was conceptualized as a continuous and relative property.
To quantify this property, we used two statistical indices.
The first was AC, defined as the lag-1 autocorrelation.

A lower AC indicates weaker temporal autocorrelation of symptom states, reflecting a relatively higher dynamic speed and potentially faster state-to-state changes (i.e., lower inertia; Kuppens et al., 2010), and thus a tendency toward a relatively faster variable.

text.text: In contrast, a higher AC indicates greater state persistence and a relatively lower dynamic speed, and thus a tendency toward a relatively slower variable.
The second index was the mean period (MP) derived from spectral power analysis (Warner, 1998), which characterizes the periodic components of fluctuations.
text.formatted: The second index was the mean period (MP) derived from spectral power analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Warner, 1998)</ref>, which characterizes the periodic components of fluctuations.

text.text: In simple terms, MP estimates the average length of a symptom's fluctuation cycle: a shorter MP means the symptom tends to rise and fall more quickly over time.

A shorter mean period indicates a relatively higher symptom dynamic speed and a tendency toward a relatively faster variable, whereas a longer mean period indicates a relatively lower dynamic speed and a tendency toward a relatively slower variable.

Spectral power analysis is based on the principle of the Fourier transform, which decomposes a time series into periodic components at different frequencies and estimates the contribution of each frequency in terms of power (Jamalabadi et al., 2025; Ruf, 1999; Zechmeister & Kürster, 2009).

text.text: Specifically, for each participant-symptom time series, observation times were converted to relative times with respect to the date (or hour) of the first observation, with the first observation set to time zero.
The Lomb-Scargle power spectrum was then calculated directly from the resulting time series.
We subsequently calculated the power-weighted mean frequency, took its reciprocal, and converted it to days to obtain MP as an index of the average fluctuation cycle of the symptom time series.

To distinguish the sources of variability in the two dynamic speed indices (AC and MP)-namely, person differences, symptom differences, and their interaction-it was necessary to account for the estimation uncertainty of the extracted features.

Although conventional variance decomposition can quantify these sources of variability, it does not explicitly account for the uncertainty associated with estimating each index from a finite time series.
We therefore estimated the standard error (SE) of each index for every personsymptom combination.
For AC, the SE could be directly calculated using the asymptotic approximation for a correlation coefficient.
Because the SE of MP could not be directly obtained from its estimation procedure, we used a block bootstrap procedure (Künsch, 1989) to estimate it.

text.text: The block length was set at the dataset level as median ( N ) 1 / 3 /median( f ) (Hall et al., 1995), where median N is the median number of observations per person-symptom cell and median f is the median sampling frequency (observations per day) per cell.

text.text: All cells within a dataset shared the same block length.
This approach allowed the blocks to retain sufficient autocorrelation structure while avoiding overly long blocks that would leave too few resampling blocks for each individual.

For cells involving multiple assessments within a single day, the relative temporal order and actual time intervals between observations within each block were retained when constructing the blocks, thereby preserving the temporal dependence structure as much as possible.
For each person-symptom combination, 2,000 bootstrap resamples were generated.
The SE of MP was then estimated as the standard deviation of the resulting bootstrap distribution.
We then fitted a multilevel meta-analytic model using the metafor package in R (Viechtbauer, 2010).
text.formatted: We then fitted a multilevel meta-analytic model using the metafor package in R <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Viechtbauer, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Although this framework is commonly used for meta-analysis, our aim here was not to synthesize effect sizes across independent studies, but to decompose variability in dynamic speed across persons, symptoms, and their combinations while accounting for the estimation uncertainty of each index.
For each dynamic speed index, the estimated index value was treated as the observed effect size, and its squared SE was specified as the sampling variance.
Person, symptom, and person-by-symptom interaction were included as crossed random effects.
This specification allowed us to quantify the overall contributions of these three sources of variability, rather than estimate differences among specific predefined symptoms.
The variance components were estimated using restricted maximum likelihood (REML), and the proportion of the total modeled variance attributable to each component was calculated.
Finally, we used the estimated variance-covariance matrix of the variance components to conduct pairwise linear contrasts.

Wald-based standard errors, 95% confidence intervals, and significance tests were calculated to assess differences between variance components and to determine whether person differences, symptom differences, or their interaction accounted for relatively more variability in dynamic speed.

As a robustness check, we repeated the variance decomposition analyses after applying a Fisher's z transformation to AC (z =tanh -1 AC) and a log transformation to MP ( log MP), to examine whether the results were sensitive to the distributional shapes of the dynamic speed indices.

text.text: The present study drew on five longitudinal experience sampling datasets and used time series of multiple psychopathological symptoms reported repeatedly by individuals over time.

Using two indices, AC and MP, we examined the variability in and sources of the dynamic speed of psychopathological symptoms, with a focus on symptom differences, person differences, and person-by-symptom interactions.

The most robust finding was that symptom differences did not explain variability in the dynamic speed of psychopathological symptoms; that is, there was little evidence that certain symptoms are consistently faster (shorter cycles; fast variables) or slower (longer cycles; slow variables) than others.
This is consistent with critiques of traditional approaches to classifying psychopathological symptoms (e.g., the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders [5th ed., text rev.
; DSM-5-TR; American Psychiatric Association, 2022]) that assume symptom attributes are relatively consistent across individuals (i.e., groupconsistent; Fried, 2020; Kotov et al., 2017).
text.formatted: ; DSM-5-TR; American Psychiatric Association, 2022]) that assume symptom attributes are relatively consistent across individuals (i.e., groupconsistent; Fried, 2020; <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Kotov et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Although such critiques have often focused on symptom-level patterns-for example, some individuals show co-occurring depression and anxiety whereas others do not-suggesting that symptom attributes may differ across individuals, our results provide evidence from a different dynamic property: dynamic speed.
By contrast, person differences may explain variability in the dynamic speed of psychopathological symptoms.

This aligns with the growing emphasis on idiographic approaches in clinical psychology (Fisher et al., 2017; Molenaar, 2004; Nemesure et al., 2024; Piccirillo & Rodebaugh, 2019; Reeves & Fisher, 2020; Wright & Woods, 2020).
text.formatted: This aligns with the growing emphasis on idiographic approaches in clinical psychology <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Fisher et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Molenaar, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Nemesure et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Piccirillo & Rodebaugh, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Reeves & Fisher, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Wright & Woods, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: However, this should not be interpreted simply as stable person-level traits determining whether all symptoms are fast or slow-that is, one person being fast across all symptoms and another being slow across all symptoms.
Results from some datasets suggested possible person-by-symptom interactions.

In summary, these findings suggest that, when examining the dynamic speed of psychopathological symptoms, it may be necessary to adopt an idiographic perspective and attend to individual-specific symptom differences.

Although longitudinal experience sampling allows the dynamic speed of psychopathological symptoms to be quantified and compared using AC and MP, the clinical implications of these differences remain to be explored.

From a dynamical systems perspective, slow variables may be particularly important because they can shape or constrain changes in fast variables and their responses to external perturbations over longer time scales, thereby influencing system stability and state transitions (Carpenter & Turner, 2000; DiFrisco, 2017; Hasselman, 2023; Walker et al., 2012).

text.text: Taking the PTSD system in the Reeves dataset as an example, if "avoidance" is identified as the relatively slowest symptom for an individual in clinical settings, an important question is whether this indicates that the symptom plays a more critical role in the system and should therefore be prioritized or given greater attention in PTSD intervention or relapse prevention.
This question may be considered in relation to the control parameters that influence the stability and overall dynamics of the system (Cui et al., 2025; Olthof et al., 2023).

text.text: In psychopathology, control parameters can be conceptualized through a stress-vulnerability framework, in which external stressors and internal vulnerabilities jointly constrain the dynamics of the system (Hankin & Abela, 2005).
text.formatted: In psychopathology, control parameters can be conceptualized through a stress-vulnerability framework, in which external stressors and internal vulnerabilities jointly constrain the dynamics of the system <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Hankin & Abela, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Given that these constraints are deeply intertwined within a personenvironment system (Olthof et al., 2023), a key empirical question is whether relatively slowdynamic PTSD symptoms are more strongly constrained by global control parameters, and whether they could serve as observable markers of this stress-vulnerability interplay.

text.text: Further empirical research is therefore needed to establish the clinical significance of the dynamic speed of psychopathological symptoms.
The present study has several limitations, which also suggest potential directions for future research.

First, although many researchers have emphasized that psychopathological systems should be conceptualized as open systems (Robinaugh et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026), the boundaries of the psychopathological systems represented in the five datasets were not consistent across datasets.

text.text: For example, the Reeves dataset focused primarily on PTSD symptoms, whereas other datasets included symptoms that may span multiple disorders, such as depression and anxiety in the Fisher dataset and Dataset E. In addition, some symptoms in certain datasets may be relatively broad and may be relevant to multiple disorders.

For example, in the Bailon dataset, "current affect" (i.e., overall good versus bad, rather than specific emotions as assessed in some disorder-specific measures) and "subjective physical activity" may both be relevant to depression, anxiety, and bipolar disorder (American Psychiatric Association, 2022).

Nevertheless, despite differences in system boundaries and symptom composition across datasets, some broadly similar patterns emerged in the sources of variance in dynamic speed, which may offer tentative support for the robustness and generalizability of our findings.
Future studies should more explicitly define the boundaries and constituent components of the psychopathological systems under investigation.
Second, the five datasets differed substantially in their measurement intervals.

In particular, Dataset E and the Wang dataset did not include multiple assessments per day, which may have obscured short-term fluctuations and limited our ability to detect differences in dynamic speed occurring over relatively short time scales.
This may partly explain why MP tended to be larger in these datasets than in datasets with more frequent measurements.

Nevertheless, despite this difference in sampling frequency, the variance decomposition results revealed some broadly similar patterns across datasets, which may provide tentative support for the robustness of our main findings.
Importantly, AC and MP are not the only possible indices of dynamic speed.
Future research should develop and evaluate additional measures of dynamic speed and examine whether the present findings can be replicated using alternative operationalizations.
Third, the present study relied exclusively on self-reported measures of psychopathological symptoms.

Self-report measures are inherently subjective and, in intensive longitudinal designs, cannot provide continuous coverage of psychopathological symptoms because frequent assessments may increase participant burden and affect compliance and data quality (Wrzus & Neubauer, 2023).
text.formatted: Self-report measures are inherently subjective and, in intensive longitudinal designs, cannot provide continuous coverage of psychopathological symptoms because frequent assessments may increase participant burden and affect compliance and data quality <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Wrzus & Neubauer, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, active self-report is generally limited to periods when participants are awake and able to respond, making it difficult to capture psychopathological symptom dynamics during sleep.

In contrast, wearable devices can continuously collect physiological and behavioral signals in daily life, including heart rate, heart rate variability, electrodermal activity, skin temperature, and physical activity, which may provide complementary information about psychopathological symptoms and their dynamics (Elgendi et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In contrast, wearable devices can continuously collect physiological and behavioral signals in daily life, including heart rate, heart rate variability, electrodermal activity, skin temperature, and physical activity, which may provide complementary information about psychopathological symptoms and their dynamics <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Elgendi et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Future research could therefore integrate wearable sensing with intensive longitudinal self-report to further examine the physiological basis of individual and symptom differences in the dynamic speed of psychopathological symptoms.
